source_evidence.anchor: Theorem 2.2.6 (Hoeffding's inequality for general bounded random variables), from its independent bounded hypotheses through its displayed upper-tail inequality
source_evidence.observation: For independent random variables X_1,...,X_N with X_i in [m_i,M_i] for every i, and every t>0, the theorem displays P{sum_{i=1}^N (X_i-E X_i) >= t} <= exp(-2 t^2 / sum_{i=1}^N (M_i-m_i)^2). The right-hand side has no leading multiplicative prefactor.

source_evidence.anchor: Definition 2.5.6, equations (2.13), (2.14), and (2.16), and Example 2.5.8(c), equation (2.17)
source_evidence.observation: The source defines ||X||_{psi_2}=inf{t>0 : E exp(X^2/t^2)<=2}; states a two-sided sub-gaussian tail with leading factor 2 and absolute exponent constant c; states the mean-zero MGF characterization up to an absolute constant; and records that every bounded X is sub-gaussian with ||X||_{psi_2} <= C||X||_infinity, where C=1/sqrt(ln 2).

For independent, mean-zero, sub-gaussian X_1,...,X_N, a=(a_1,...,a_N) in R^N, and every t>=0, the theorem states P{|sum_{i=1}^N a_i X_i| >= t} <= 2 exp(-c t^2/(K^2 ||a||_2^2)), where K=max_i ||X_i||_{psi_2}; the surrounding sub-gaussian bounds identify c as an absolute positive constant.

The exercise asks the reader to deduce bounded-variable Hoeffding, specifically Theorem 2.2.6, from Theorem 2.6.3, while permitting some absolute constant in place of 2 in the exponent. It does not permit adding a leading prefactor.

The prose says to apply 'Theorem 2.6.3' to a_i X_i before Theorem 2.6.3 itself is stated. Structurally, this is an editorial self-reference; the displayed theorem that follows is nevertheless unambiguous.

binders: A finite positive index size N, implicit in the notation X_1,...,X_N and in max_i in Theorem 2.6.3. [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; Theorem 2.6.3.]
Real-valued random variables X_1,...,X_N and real interval endpoints m_i,M_i for i=1,...,N. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
A real deviation threshold t with t>0 for the bounded-variable conclusion. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]

An absolute positive exponent constant c_0, globally independent of N, t, the laws of the X_i, and the interval endpoints; Exercise 2.6.4 permits c_0 in place of the displayed constant 2. [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; Exercise 2.6.4; PDF p. 6, printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
hypotheses: The random variables X_1,...,X_N are independent. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
For every i, the source writes X_i in [m_i,M_i]; in the probabilistic setting this is the bounded-support hypothesis. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
No mean-zero hypothesis is imposed on the original bounded variables; the quantity in the event centers each variable as X_i-E X_i. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
The source does not explicitly assume sum_i (M_i-m_i)^2>0. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; complete hypotheses and displayed denominator of Theorem 2.2.6.]
conclusions: Writing V=sum_{i=1}^N (M_i-m_i)^2, deduce P{sum_{i=1}^N (X_i-E X_i) >= t} <= exp(-c_0 t^2/V), with no leading multiplicative prefactor; Theorem 2.2.6 has c_0=2, and Exercise 2.6.4 explicitly allows another absolute c_0. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6; PDF p. 18, printed p. 29; Exercise 2.6.4.]
definitions_and_conventions: The psi_2 norm is ||X||_{psi_2}=inf{u>0 : E exp(X^2/u^2)<=2}. [PDF p. 16; printed p. 27; Definition 2.5.6 and (2.13).]
Every bounded random variable X is sub-gaussian and satisfies ||X||_{psi_2} <= (1/sqrt(ln 2))||X||_infinity. [PDF p. 16; printed p. 27; Example 2.5.8(c) and (2.17).]
In Theorem 2.6.3, ||a||_2^2=sum_i a_i^2 and K=max_i ||X_i||_{psi_2}; the tail event is two-sided because it contains the absolute value of the weighted sum. [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; Theorem 2.6.3.]

The constants denoted C,c in the sub-gaussian estimates are absolute and positive; Exercise 2.6.4 uses the same 'absolute constant' convention for the replacement exponent coefficient. [PDF p. 16; printed p. 27; text following (2.16); PDF p. 18, printed p. 29; Exercise 2.6.4.]
Theorem 2.2.6 uses a one-sided event and t>0, whereas Theorem 2.6.3 uses a two-sided absolute-value event and t>=0. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6; PDF p. 18, printed p. 29; Theorem 2.6.3.]
implicit_context: The source route is to center the bounded variables, rescale each nonzero-width coordinate by d_i=M_i-m_i, use weights a_i=d_i, and invoke the bounded-implies-sub-gaussian estimate so that K is uniformly bounded and ||a||_2^2=sum_i d_i^2. This reduction is analyst inference from the centered target, (2.17), and Theorem 2.6.3, not an explicit derivation printed in Exercise 2.6.4. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6; PDF p. 16, printed p. 27; (2.17); PDF p. 18, printed p. 29; Theorem 2.6.3 and Exercise 2.6.4.]

A single application of Theorem 2.6.3 gives at best a leading factor 2 after passing from the two-sided event to the desired upper-tail event. Independent-copy tensorization supplies the missing no-prefactor generation: for r independent copies, p^r <= 2 exp(-r c_1 t^2/V), hence p <= 2^(1/r) exp(-c_1 t^2/V), and r to infinity removes 2. This is analyst inference, not a method stated in the exercise. [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; displayed leading factor 2 in Theorem 2.6.3 and the no-prefactor cross-reference in Exercise 2.6.4; PDF p. 6, printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]

Coordinates with d_i=0 can be omitted in the rescaling argument because their centered terms vanish under the standard bounded-support reading; if every d_i=0, the tail event is impossible for t>0, but the source's displayed quotient has denominator zero. This is analyst inference about the source boundary, not an explicit source case split. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6 and its displayed denominator.]

details: The requested bounded-variable inequality is upper-tail only and quantifies t>0. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
The supplying general inequality is two-sided and permits t=0. [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; Theorem 2.6.3.]
The target has exactly exp(-c_0 t^2/V), with implicit leading factor 1. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6; PDF p. 18, printed p. 29; Exercise 2.6.4.]

Theorem 2.6.3 has leading factor 2. Exercise 2.6.4 licenses changing only the numerical coefficient 2 in the exponent to an absolute constant, not changing the target to 2 exp(-c_0 t^2/V). [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; Theorem 2.6.3 and Exercise 2.6.4.]

Independent-copy tensorization is an analyst-inferred way to obtain the required leading factor 1 from Theorem 2.6.3 without changing the exponent's absolute-constant character. [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; Theorem 2.6.3 and Exercise 2.6.4; PDF p. 6, printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
The denominator required by Theorem 2.2.6 is the sum of individual squared interval widths, not N times the largest squared width. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; displayed inequality in Theorem 2.2.6.]

Theorem 2.6.3 separates a uniform psi_2 bound K from the Euclidean weight norm, enabling the analyst-inferred choice a_i=M_i-m_i after coordinatewise normalization. [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; Theorem 2.6.3; PDF p. 16, printed p. 27; bounded example (2.17).]
The conclusion concerns the centered summands X_i-E X_i even though the original X_i need not have mean zero. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
Mean zero is mandatory in Theorem 2.6.3, so centering is part of the inferred reduction. [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; Theorem 2.6.3; PDF p. 6, printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
The source states no strict-width or positive-total-width hypothesis. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; complete hypothesis list of Theorem 2.2.6.]

When all M_i=m_i, the centered sum vanishes under the standard bounded-support reading, but the printed expression divides by sum_i (M_i-m_i)^2=0; the source gives no explicit extended-real convention or separate case. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; displayed inequality in Theorem 2.2.6.]

undebatable_constraints: The audit claim is the Exercise 2.6.4 directive to derive Theorem 2.2.6 from Theorem 2.6.3, not merely a generic bounded-variable concentration statement. [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; Exercise 2.6.4.]
The desired probability event is P{sum_i (X_i-E X_i) >= t}, with independent bounded X_i and t>0. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
The variance proxy in the denominator is exactly sum_i (M_i-m_i)^2. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
The desired right-hand side has no leading multiplicative prefactor. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; displayed inequality in Theorem 2.2.6.]

The exact coefficient 2 in the exponent may be replaced by an unspecified absolute positive constant, but the exercise does not authorize dependence on N, t, the distributions, or the endpoints. [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; Exercise 2.6.4.]
Theorem 2.6.3 itself is a two-sided absolute-value bound with leading factor 2, denominator K^2||a||_2^2, and K=max_i ||X_i||_{psi_2}. [PDF p. 18; printed p. 29; Theorem 2.6.3.]
The source includes no explicit exclusion or interpretation of the case sum_i (M_i-m_i)^2=0. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; complete Theorem 2.2.6.]

ambiguities.issue: The immediate corollary of the displayed Theorem 2.6.3 retains a leading factor 2, while the cross-referenced Theorem 2.2.6 has leading factor 1 and Exercise 2.6.4 permits changing only the exponent constant.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 18, printed page 29, Theorem 2.6.3 displays 2 exp(-c t^2/(K^2||a||_2^2)); Exercise 2.6.4 names Theorem 2.2.6 and mentions only an absolute constant replacing 2 in the exponent. PDF page 6, printed page 17, Theorem 2.2.6 displays exp(-2t^2/V).
ambiguities.impact: A one-shot application plus event inclusion does not establish the literal target. Independent-copy tensorization can remove the prefactor, but that argument is analyst inference and is not stated in the exercise.

ambiguities.issue: The all-zero-width case is included by the written hypotheses but makes the displayed exponent divide by zero.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 6, printed page 17, Theorem 2.2.6 assumes only X_i in [m_i,M_i] and displays denominator sum_i (M_i-m_i)^2, without a positivity side condition or a convention for zero denominator.
ambiguities.impact: A literal ordinary-real formulation needs a separate V=0 branch or an explicit extended-real convention. Adding V>0 globally would omit a source-allowed degenerate family, even though its t>0 tail event is trivial under the standard bounded-support reading.

ambiguities.issue: The notation X_i in [m_i,M_i] does not explicitly say 'almost surely' or state m_i<=M_i.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 6, printed page 17, the complete boundedness hypothesis in Theorem 2.2.6 is written only as 'Assume that X_i in [m_i,M_i] for every i.'
ambiguities.impact: The standard probabilistic reading is an almost-sure bound by a nonempty interval, but a formal target must choose that measure-theoretic interpretation explicitly.

ambiguities.issue: The prose introducing Theorem 2.6.3 refers to applying Theorem 2.6.3 before that theorem is stated.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 18, printed page 29, the paragraph immediately before Theorem 2.6.3 says 'let us apply Theorem 2.6.3 for a_i X_i instead of X_i.'
ambiguities.impact: This appears to be an editorial self-reference, naturally read as referring to the immediately preceding Theorem 2.6.2. It does not change the complete displayed statement of Theorem 2.6.3 used by Exercise 2.6.4.

contract_plain_english: Exercise 2.6.4 asks for the exact one-sided bounded-variable Hoeffding form from Theorem 2.2.6, except that the numerical 2 multiplying t^2 in the exponent may be replaced by any universal positive constant. Thus independent X_i bounded in [m_i,M_i] must satisfy, for t>0, P{sum_i(X_i-E X_i)>=t} <= exp(-c_0 t^2/sum_i(M_i-m_i)^2), with no leading factor 2. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6; PDF p. 18, printed p. 29; Exercise 2.6.4.] Theorem 2.6.3 supplies a two-sided bound with a leading 2 for weighted independent mean-zero sub-gaussians; boundedness and coordinatewise width normalization produce the correct squared-width denominator, and an independent-copy tensorization argument can remove the leading 2. Those reduction details are analyst inference rather than text printed in the exercise. [PDF p. 16; printed p. 27; Definition 2.5.6 and (2.17); PDF p. 18, printed p. 29; Theorem 2.6.3.] The source does not explicitly resolve the case in which every interval has zero width, where the centered tail is trivial for t>0 but the displayed exponent has denominator zero. [PDF p. 6; printed p. 17; Theorem 2.2.6.]
